cows fed an anionic diet (22 meq/100g of diet DM) had lower incidence and severity of hypocalcemia at calving than did cows fed a cationic diet (126 meq/ 100g of diet).
cows fed an anionic (low cation:high anion) diet were protected from parturient hypoclacemia.

feeding anionic diets containing high concentrations of Cl and low concentrations of Na to Jersey cows during the last month of pregnancy and for 1 d after parturition reduces incidence and severity of hypocalcemia at parturition.

the effect of dietary cation to anions ratio on the incidence of parturient paresis (milk fever) and the associated metabolic changes.
the effects of dietary anions on the incidence and severity of hypocalcemia and on the concentrations of Ca and other electrolytes in plasma and milk of dairy cows.
the effect of feeding anionic diets on the incidence and severity of hypocalcemia and on the incidence of retained placenta in dairy cows.

feeding a diet with a high cation:anion balance (diet 3) to Jersey cows during the dry period reduced the severity of parturition hypocalcemia and the incidence of milk fever in the postpartum period, and feeding a diet with an intermediate cation:an ion balance (diet 2) to Jersey cows had no significant effect on the severity of parturtition hypocalcemic.
dietary Cl, as part of a cation-anion ratio, may be a useful tool in the prevention of parturient paresis in dairy cows.
dietary cation-anions are effective in the prevention of hypocalcemia and that the addition of Cl is an effective way to alter the cation-anion ratio.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the addition of Cl to the diet in the form of NaCl, KCl, and/or CaCl 2, or a combination thereof, can effectively reduce the incidence and severity of milk fever.
feeding anionic diets to cows 6 wk prior to parturition reduced the incidence and severity of hypocalcemia during parturition.
feeding cows a diet with a high cation-anion ratio (diet 3) reduced the incidence of parturient paresis and increased the incidence of milk fever.
The main takeaway from our work is that
feeding anionic diets can reduce the incidence and severity of milk fever in dairy cows.
feeding a cation-anion balanced ration to Jersey cows during late pregnancy and early lactation can reduce the risk of milk fever.
the use of anionic salts to reduce milk fever in Jersey cows fed alfalfa forage-based diets is an effective management strategy.
